newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bond yields rebound, CPI not weak enough.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond yields rebound, CPI not weak enough.

text.p: *Australian bond yields rebounded from their initial lows after a pretty benign March quarter inflation report was not weak enough for the market to rally further.
*The market had been looking for an even lower result.
Australian bond yields rebounded from their initial lows as profit-takers quickly stepped in after a pretty benign March quarter inflation report proved insufficient for the market to rally further.

"The market had psyched itself up for a better than expected result. The fact that it has come in on expectations is probably a bit of a disappointment," said Michael Blythe, senior economist at Commonwealth bank of Australia.
The 10-year bond yield had sunk to around 7.75 percent before the data incontinuation of Tuesday's rally after Tuesday's moderate low-pay award and firm U.S. Treasuries.

Headline inflation rose 0.2 percent to an annual 1.3 percent, its lowest annual rate for four years. The policy sensitive underlying rate rose 0.4 percent for a year-on-year rate of 2.1 percent and remaining at the low end of the Reserve Bank 2.0-3.0 percent target.

"The market set itself a very tough target to get a positive response," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia. "There are a couple of high quarterly figures to drop out of the year-on-year rate run...so we are going to be sub-2.0 percent next quarter. That's the sort of stuff that should help the long end, but not necessarily result in another rate cut."

There has been speculation that after the Australian Industrial Relations Commission awarded just A$10 per week to low paid workers, a weak inflation outcome would leave the Reserve Bank scope to ease policy again if it felt that the economy needed a further stimulus.

"You can certainly make a case for another easing. But given that the stimulus from previous rate cuts are still to flow through, we don't think the RBA will be rushing in to do anything," CBA's Blythe said.
June bill futures eased back with bond contracts to 94.10 from a high of 94.17, it highest level since mid-February.
But even accounting for this setback, the contract is still equating to a cash rate of 5.90 percent and below current 6.0 percent official interest rates.

The early rally in bonds was also helped by an advance in U.S. Treasuries after a solid response to a two year note auction and amid hopes for an agreement between the Clinton administration and Republican leaders on a balanced budget.
Although local debt outperformed the U.S. move before the inflation data, this was quickly reversed after the report leaving spread differentials wider on the day.
The local market also turned around against Canadian and New Zealand bonds after an initial spread tightening.
The domestic yield curve flattened as the short end underperformed after the inflation data and practically wiping Tuesday's steepening on the AIRC wage result.
